What We Publish

What question did we ask? What did we find? And why does it matter?

Can wind and solar power reliably meet electricity demand?

Not on their own. Wind- and solar-only systems sized to match annual electricity demand meet roughly 72-91% of hourly demand in most countries, and 83-94% with twelve hours of storage — leaving hundreds of hours of unmet demand each year even in the best cases. The residual gap is set by the geophysics of the atmosphere, so closing it requires storage, demand flexibility, long-distance transmission, or firm generation rather than more wind and solar capacity alone.

Identification of reliable locations for wind power generation through a global analysis of wind droughts

Antonini et al., 2024 · Communications Earth & Environment

Wind droughts are least limiting in the American Midwest, Australia, the Sahara, Argentina, Central Asia, and Southern Africa; across most of the world there is little evidence of strong trends in wind droughts in recent decades, and the most severe droughts in many places occurred before wind power was a substantial part of the electricity supply.

Geophysical constraints on the reliability of solar and wind power worldwide

Tong et al., 2021 · Nature Communications

Using 39 years of hourly weather data for 42 countries, the most reliable wind- and solar-only electricity systems — with annual generation equal to annual demand and no storage — met 72-91% of hourly electricity demand, rising to 83-94% with 12 hours of storage.

Other papers

Historical model biases in monthly high temperature anomalies indicate under-estimation of future temperature extremes

Duan et al., 2025 · Communications Earth & Environment

CMIP6 models have underestimated 22-year-average monthly high-temperature anomalies by 2-3% and 22-year maximum anomalies by 11-12%; if those historical biases carry forward, average 2100 extreme high temperatures in some regions and months could exceed current projections by 3 K, and by more than 5 K in the most extreme cases.

Climate change as an incentive for future human migration

Chen and Caldeira, 2020 · Earth System Dynamics

Analysing today's relationship between climate and population density with all other factors held constant, climate change may within decades give hundreds of millions of people additional incentive to migrate, largely from warm tropical and subtropical countries towards cooler temperate countries, with India the country with the greatest number of people so affected.

Insensitivity of global warming potentials to carbon dioxide emission scenarios

Caldeira and Kasting, 1993 · Nature

Global warming potentials are largely insensitive to the carbon dioxide emission scenario assumed, because two effects of higher CO2 concentrations work in opposite directions: each additional molecule of CO2 produces less radiative forcing than the last, while the atmospheric lifetime of that CO2 grows as the ocean's capacity to absorb it saturates.
